name: Hyaluronidase filler dissolving

lead: Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that break down hyaluronic acid, the main ingredient of most popular dermal fillers. In aesthetics it is injected to dissolve filler that looks lumpy, bluish or overfilled under thin skin, notably under the eyes, so the contour can be corrected. Wikipedia calls it the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler.

It breaks the bonds in hyaluronic acid, lowering viscosity and increasing tissue permeability. It does not act on non-HA fillers such as calcium hydroxyapatite. It has long been used in medicine to help injected drugs spread; registered trials found address eye surgery, anesthesia blocks and other uses rather than filler dissolving.

paras: Clinicians inject it into the area with unwanted filler, and people use it to reset an under-eye contour or fix complications. Results begin to show as the filler breaks down, and it is sometimes followed by re-treatment with filler.

Local reactions include pain, swelling and itching; systemic effects and rare hypersensitivity are reported (incidence about 0.05 to 0.69 percent per Grokipedia). Animal-derived and recombinant products differ in immunogenicity.

web.title: Is It Really Safe to Dissolve Your Fillers? - VICE

angle.text: Hyaluronidase dissolves hyaluronic acid filler that looks lumpy, bluish or overfilled, notably under the eyes, so the contour can be visibly corrected. The enzyme breaks down the filler and the area returns toward its natural shape. It is established medicine; trials of filler dissolving specifically are limited.

lead: Hyaluronidase is a family of enzymes that degrade hyaluronic acid (HA), a component of the extracellular matrix.[1] By lowering the viscosity of HA, it increases tissue permeability, which helps injected substances disperse.[2]

For appearance, its value is reversibility. Most popular dermal fillers are made of cross-linked HA, so an injector can inject hyaluronidase into a lumpy, overfilled, asymmetric or bluish-looking area and let the enzyme break the gel down, returning the face toward its earlier shape.[2][3] It is also the standard drug named in aesthetic guidelines for treating filler complications such as vascular occlusion.[3] Wikipedia calls it the best treatment option for dissolving lip filler.[2]

Fillers not based on HA are not dissolved by it; a 2023 paper notes calcium hydroxyapatite filler cannot easily be dissolved. Laboratory and small clinical studies show that different HA fillers respond differently to the enzyme depending on their cross-linking and particle design.[4][5][6]

Dissolving has become a visible part of aesthetic culture. The Aesthetic Society first reported US filler-reversal figures in 2020, with more than 14,000 reversals, and the count rose 57 percent the following year to over 23,000, according to VICE [7]. NewBeauty described a 2022 uptick in people dissolving filler and sometimes refilling the area, with lips and tear troughs the most commonly treated sites [8].
Most published trials of hyaluronidase concern other uses such as eye surgery, nerve blocks and as a drug-spreading agent.[9]
infobox: HYAL1 to HYAL5 (PH-20) and a pseudogene HYAL6
Hyaluronic acid fillers only; not calcium hydroxyapatite, Sculptra or neuromodulators [8]
Off-label; FDA has not approved a product for removing dermal fillers [7]

paras: Established uses include ophthalmic surgery with local anesthetics, subcutaneous fluid absorption (hypodermoclysis) and subcutaneous urography.[2] The enzyme is also used to treat extravasation of hyperosmolar solutions and has been recommended in vinca alkaloid extravasation.[2]

Recombinant human hyaluronidase PH20 (Halozyme's ENHANZE technology) is co-formulated with several biologic drugs so larger volumes can be given under the skin, for example trastuzumab, rituximab and immunoglobulin products, and the subcutaneous breast cancer product Phesgo.[10][11]

In aesthetic practice the enzyme is injected to dissolve HA filler when product looks lumpy or bluish beneath thin skin (sometimes described as a Tyndall-type discoloration), when a result is asymmetric or overdone, or when complications such as vascular occlusion occur.[1][2][3] A 2021 guideline in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology describes it as a drug that has gained widespread use in aesthetic medicine to dissolve HA-based fillers, and sets out indications, formulation differences, adverse events and allergy considerations.[3]

Lip filler is the best-known case. Proponents of reversibility often cite hyaluronidase as the reason HA fillers are described as forgiving: if a patient is unhappy, the product can be removed rather than waited out.[2] Fillers that last longer or are not HA-based, such as calcium hydroxyapatite, do not share this option.

Mammalian hyaluronidases cleave beta-1,4 bonds in HA, producing smaller fragments.[1] Most HA fillers are cross-linked to slow breakdown in the body, which also changes how readily the enzyme can reach and cut the gel.[12]

In vitro work comparing animal-derived ovine hyaluronidase (Vitrase) and human recombinant hyaluronidase (Hylenex) on four commercial fillers found that Restylane dissipated most, followed by Juvederm, while Belotero retained its form best, and that the response grew over the first five minutes.[5] A laser particle-size study of Restylane, Juvederm Voluma and Belotero Balance measured how much each cross-linked gel was digested by available hyaluronidase preparations.[6]

Four purified hyaluronidases are approved in the US: ovine (Vitrase), bovine (Amphadase, Hydase) and the human recombinant Hylenex.[2] Animal-extracted products have been used for decades to increase dispersion of co-administered drugs.[13]

Dermal fillers carry known risks beyond cosmetic dissatisfaction. Wikipedia describes vascular occlusion, in which filler enters a blood vessel and can cause delayed skin necrosis or, through retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries, vision loss that is usually permanent when it occurs; embolic complications are described as more common with autologous fat, followed by hyaluronic acid.[12] Allergic reactions to fillers may leave scarring and lumps that can need surgical correction.[12] Because the enzyme acts on HA gel directly, aesthetic guidelines name it as the drug for treating HA-filler complications such as vascular compromise, and the 2021 guideline in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology includes a modified high-dose protocol for that situation.[3]

In the United States the FDA regulates dermal fillers as medical devices, with a provider prescribing and performing the injection; in the EU and UK they need a CE mark, which confirms production standards rather than medical efficacy.[12] Hyaluronidase itself is a prescription medicine, and its aesthetic use for dissolving filler is an off-label application of products approved for other purposes such as increasing dispersion and absorption of other injected drugs.[2][3]

Wikipedia notes that fillers are mostly temporary because the body gradually metabolizes them, typically lasting around six months for many products, with duration varying by filler type, skin, injector and how active the treated area is; cross-linking prolongs retention.[12] Dissolving with the enzyme is therefore a way to shorten a result rather than wait for natural breakdown.[2][12]

The FDA's consumer page on dermal fillers calls unintentional injection into a blood vessel the most concerning risk, listing tissue death, vision abnormalities including blindness, and stroke among reported complications, and advises people to seek immediate care for unusual pain, vision changes or white, gray or blue skin near the injection site [14]. An FDA spokesperson told VICE the agency had not approved any product for removing dermal fillers [7].

A NewBeauty feature published in April 2022 reports reasons patients give for dissolving filler: overfilled or plastic-looking results, lumps, migrating product, dissatisfaction with a provider's work, and changing goals as they age [8]. Dermatologist Ellen Marmur credits TikTok with sparking the craze to reverse HA fillers [8].

The same article describes the notion of filler fatigue, in which repeated expansion and relaxation of tissue is said to make filler less effective over time; plastic surgeon Leo McCafferty notes in it that the idea is debatable [8]. After dissolving, patients can leave the area as it is or refill it, and dermatologist Valerie Callender recommends reinjecting in stages [8]. Alternatives mentioned include fat transfer, neuromodulator lip flips and an extracellular-matrix product [8].
VICE reported that Kylie Jenner had her lip filler dissolved in 2018, and that celebrity reversals are widely associated with the shift toward more natural-looking lips [7].

A VICE investigation published in August 2022 collected accounts from patients who reported burning skin, volume loss, nerve pain, dry eye, headaches and fatigue after hyaluronidase treatment, and an online support group of more than 2,000 members discusses such effects; the article notes there is no clinical data establishing a causal link [7].

Clinicians quoted in the piece gave differing views. Plastic surgeon Ben Talei said remote changes from facial hyaluronidase are exceedingly unlikely, dermatologist Derek Jones said he had treated thousands of patients over 16 years without seeing the problems described, and oculoplastic surgeon Daniel Ezra said a small proportion of patients end up worse off but attributed lasting damage mainly to the filler itself [7]. Former American Society of Plastic Surgeons president Dr Matarasso said there is no standard training for this use and that practitioners should use the smallest effective volume [7].

Some clinicians also note that the enzyme breaks down the skin's own hyaluronic acid as well as filler, and Talei said recovery can take weeks or, for some people, one to three years [7]. The Australian TGA reported seven adverse event reports involving hyaluronidase since 2015, relating to anaphylaxis and allergic reactions, and said off-label use depends on the doctor's judgment and informed consent [7]. Halozyme, maker of Hylenex, does not promote it for filler reversal [7].

Related options include waiting for fillers to metabolise on their own, which typically takes around six months for many HA products [12], staged refilling, fat transfer and surgery for non-HA or permanent fillers. The FDA states that removing filler may require injections, surgery or other interventions and can be difficult or impossible, particularly for permanent and non-HA fillers [14]. Calcium hydroxyapatite filler and Sculptra do not respond to the enzyme and are left to wear off [8].

Reported effects include injection-site pain, swelling and itching, plus rarely systemic reactions; Grokipedia cites hypersensitivity incidence of about 0.05 to 0.69 percent and pre-existing antibodies to recombinant PH20 in roughly 6 percent of people.[1]

The aesthetic guideline discusses allergy to hyaluronidase, including the suggestion that allergy to wasp and bee stings is associated with higher risk, the types of allergic response, and how these relate to skin testing.[3] Clinicians sometimes express anxiety about animal-derived products for this reason, and recombinant human hyaluronidase was developed as a purer, non-foreign alternative.[3][13] Dedicated hypersensitivity studies of ovine hyaluronidase (Vitrase) have been registered.[15]

Hyaluronan is a high-molecular-mass polysaccharide found in the extracellular matrix of soft connective tissue; breaking it down lowers resistance to fluid flow in the subcutaneous space, which is the basis of the drug-delivery uses.[11] Degradation products of HA have been reported to be biologically active, including inducing angiogenesis in a 1985 study.[16]
Humans have five functional hyaluronidases (HYAL1 to HYAL4 and PH-20/HYAL5) and one pseudogene; HYAL1 and HYAL2 are the major forms in most tissues.[2]

Hyaluronidase was first used in general medicine in 1949, according to the aesthetic guideline.[3] Karl Meyer classified hyaluronidases into three groups in 1971.[2] Purified US products followed: Vitrase (May 2004), Amphadase (October 2004), Hydase (October 2005) and recombinant Hylenex (December 2005).[2]

Its aesthetic role grew with HA fillers, which spread widely after the 1980s and which regulators treat as medical devices; in the US they are placed by licensed providers, and in the EEA and UK they are non-prescription devices.[12] Combination products pairing biologics with recombinant hyaluronidase have been approved since the 2010s, including HyQvia in the EU in 2013.[2]

A randomized, masked study of 18 arms in nine subjects tested Restylane-L, Juvederm Ultra and Juvederm Voluma, each dissolved one week later with 2.5, 5, 10 or 20 units of Hylenex or compared with controls. The largest changes in diameter, elevation and firmness occurred from 30 minutes through 3 hours, with gradual degradation to week 2 and follow-up beyond four years; Voluma showed a clear dose response from 2.5 to 10 units, while a milder dose response was found for the other two gels.[4]

Safety work on the recombinant form includes a double-blind, placebo-controlled single-dose trial in 100 volunteers injected intradermally, in which no allergic reactions were observed.[13] A separate randomized trial in 100 healthy volunteers examined catheter and securement techniques for hyaluronidase-facilitated subcutaneous fluid delivery.[17]

Registered trials of the enzyme address other uses: Vitrase for vitreous hemorrhage (NCT00198510, n=750; NCT00198497, n=510), hypersensitivity to ovine hyaluronidase (NCT00198419, NCT00198458, n=65 each), as a spreading agent (NCT00198484, n=108), and as an additive to bupivacaine nerve blocks.[9][15][18]

lore.intro: Filler dissolving is discussed on social media, in patient support groups and in beauty-press coverage as the way to undo or reset filler results, with an ongoing conversation about aftereffects [7][8].

claims.claim: Hyaluronidase lets you fully undo HA filler
It can also dissolve non-HA fillers like Radiesse or Sculptra
Dissolving can cause lasting problems such as skin thinning, nerve pain or dry eye
It also dissolves your natural hyaluronic acid and can reduce hydration
Filler fatigue means filler stops working after repeated rounds, so dissolving resets the face
Dissolving is the emergency treatment for filler vascular occlusion
Allergy risk makes it unsafe, especially animal-derived versions

timeline.event: Hyaluronidase first used in general medicine.[3]
Karl Meyer classifies hyaluronidases into three groups.[2]
Vitrase and Amphadase approved in the US.[2]
HyQvia combination of immune globulin and recombinant hyaluronidase approved in the EU; the US approval follows in 2014 [2].
Hydase and recombinant Hylenex approved in the US.[2]
HyQvia (immune globulin with recombinant hyaluronidase) approved in the US.[2]
Kylie Jenner has her lip filler dissolved, reported by VICE as a high-profile example of reversal [7].
The Aesthetic Society first reports US filler reversal data: over 14,000 reversals [7].
US filler reversals reported up 57 percent to over 23,000 [7]; the 2021 guideline on safe aesthetic hyaluronidase use, including a modified high-dose protocol, is published [3].
VICE and NewBeauty publish features on filler dissolving, patient-reported effects and the dissolve-and-refill trend [7][8].
